name: Wangye (Plague Lord)
aliases: Qiansui Ye (Lord of a Thousand Years)
domain: Warding off evil, driving out plague, patrolling the human world on behalf of the Jade Emperor
description: A wooden boat that cost tens of millions to build, carved in exquisite detail, goes up in flames while tens of thousands of people look on. It isn't an accident: this is "burning the royal boat," the grandest religious ritual in southern Taiwan, and its central figures are the Wangye, the Royal Lords, also called Qiansui Ye (Lords of a Thousand Years) or Daitian Xunshou, "inspectors on Heaven's behalf." Wangye is not a single god but the name for a whole family of them: the Five Lords, the Seven Lords, the Twelve Plague Kings, and more. Taiwan has over a hundred Wangye of different surnames, clustered along the coasts of Yunlin, Chiayi, Tainan, Kaohsiung, and Pingtung, and their job is to tour the human world for the Jade Emperor and drive out plague. Donggang's Welcoming the Royal Lords ceremony in Pingtung, held once every three years, runs eight days of inviting the lords, processions, banquets, and finally the boat burning, and has been designated a national important folk custom. Nankunshen Daitian Temple is known as the head temple of Wangye in Taiwan, with branch temples all over the island. If you want to see Taiwanese folk religion at its most alive, visit a Wangye temple.
story:
Who are the Wangye? Folk tradition offers at least three answers, and every one of them has drama.

The most widespread version tells of 360 imperial scholars of the Tang dynasty who were sent on an official tour and lost at sea along the way. Moved by their loyalty, the Jade Emperor appointed them "inspectors on Heaven's behalf," to take turns descending to the human world, judging good and evil and driving out plague. That's why the Wangye have so many different surnames.

Another version ties them to Koxinga (Zheng Chenggong): his officers who fell in battle were enshrined as local guardians, and Wangye worship around Tainan and Kaohsiung is often bound up with that history.

But the version closest to ordinary people's lives is about "sending off the plague." In earlier times epidemics were the most feared disaster of all, so people gave the plague a face, the Wangye, built a real boat, loaded it with offerings, and sent it out to sea. When a royal boat drifted ashore, coastal villagers dared not neglect it. It had arrived by heaven's mandate, and it had to be welcomed into the village with all due reverence and given a temple. Many Wangye temples in Taiwan began exactly this way, with a boat that washed up on the beach.

All three stories point to the same thing: in an age without much medicine, the Wangye were people's greatest ally against plague.

temples.name: Donggang Donglong Temple
temples.deityStory: Famous for its Welcoming the Royal Lords ceremony, held once every three years. The burning of the royal boat is the climax, sending away the plague gods and evil influences and praying for peace.

temples.name: Nankunshen Daitian Temple
temples.deityStory: The head temple of Wangye in Taiwan. Its branch temples are spread across the island, crowds pour in every pilgrimage season, and the sight of spirit mediums wielding their ritual weapons is spectacular.

associatedTemples: Donggang Donglong Temple (Donggang Township, Pingtung County)
Nankunshen Daitian Temple (Beimen District, Tainan City)
worship:
Offerings to the Wangye are mainly fresh flowers, fruit, vegetarian food, and pastries; during royal boat festivals some temples also prepare the three sacrificial meats (chicken, pork, and fish). Each temple's busiest season follows the birthday of the Wangye it enshrines, and since the surnames differ, so do the dates.

The real draw at a Wangye temple is the ritual. In the incense-passing procession, the deity's statue is carried through the neighborhood and every place it passes counts as blessed. In pilgrimage (jinxiang), groups travel back to the mother temple to worship. And Wangye worship is especially known for consulting spirit mediums (jitong), who convey the god's will through their bodies; it is one of the few places in Taiwan where medium culture is still practiced frequently.

During a royal boat festival you can join the inviting of the lords, the processions, and the banquets, but keep a few things in mind: stay quiet, don't block the ritual's path, and follow the temple staff's directions. If you want to photograph a medium in trance or the burning of the boat, always ask the temple's permission first.
festivals:
The Wangye's birthdays vary by surname. Common ones include Lord Li (26th day of the 4th lunar month), Lord Chi (18th day of the 6th lunar month), and Lord Zhu (15th day of the 8th lunar month). Each temple holds its celebration on the birthday of the Wangye it enshrines.

The most representative festival is **Donggang's Welcoming the Royal Lords ceremony in Pingtung**, held once every three years (in the years of the Ox, Dragon, Goat, and Dog) and lasting eight days. The full cycle includes inviting the lords, fire-walking, processions, banqueting the lords, and burning the royal boat. It is one of Taiwan's largest religious and cultural events and has been designated a national important folk custom by the Ministry of Culture. **Xigang Qing'an Temple in Tainan** also holds a royal boat ceremony as part of the Xigang Incense Procession, once every three years, designated a national important folk custom in 2009; the royal boat festival in Mailiao, Yunlin, hosted by Kaiyuan Temple and Zhen'an Temple, takes place once every five years.

During the Lunar New Year (the first lunar month), Wangye temples also hold group New Year worship and Tai Sui rites, making it one of the liveliest times to see Wangye worship.

name: Nezha (Third Prince)
domain: Warding off evil, guardian of children, patron of the transport trade
description: Wind-fire wheels under his feet, a fire-tipped spear in his hand, and the ability to dance to electronic music in neon costume: the Third Prince may be the coolest god in the world. He is Nezha from the classic novel Investiture of the Gods, third son of Li Jing, honored in the divine world as the Marshal of the Central Altar. Unlike other gods, he is always a child: a little bib, the Universe Ring, the wind-fire wheels, and energy to spare. But don't be fooled by appearances. The Third Prince is heaven's vanguard, a fearsome fighter who always walks at the very front of temple processions, leading the way to drive off evil. At the opening ceremony of the 2009 World Games in Kaohsiung, the "Electronic Third Princes" danced to electronic music in neon god costumes and brought the house down; they went on to the Shanghai World Expo, Japan, and the United States, becoming a signature symbol of Taiwanese culture. He is also one of the few gods worshipped in the form of a child. At temple festivals, the Third Prince performers play with children and hand out candy. No god feels closer.
story:
The Third Prince's story is extraordinary from the moment he was born.

Li Jing's wife carried him for three years and six months (yes, you read that right), and what she gave birth to was a ball of flesh. Li Jing, terrified, drew his sword and split it open, and out jumped a little boy in a bib, standing on wind-fire wheels. This was Nezha.

From the start, Nezha was trouble. One day he went to bathe by the sea, threw the Dragon Palace of the Eastern Sea into chaos, and even killed the Dragon King's third son. The Dragon King came to Li Jing's door demanding the boy. With his whole family about to pay for it, Nezha did something earth-shaking: he cut away his bones to return them to his father and his flesh to return it to his mother, using his own life to sever his ties to his parents and shoulder all the blame alone.

Later the immortal Taiyi Zhenren rebuilt him a new body out of lotus flowers. From then on Nezha was no longer flesh and blood but a lotus incarnation: faster, fiercer, and stronger.

That spirit of owning what you've done is probably why Taiwanese love the Third Prince so much. He isn't perfect and he makes trouble, but he takes responsibility.

temples.name: Xinying Taizi Temple
temples.deityStory: The head temple and founding ancestral temple of the Marshal of the Central Altar, with branch temples everywhere; its old temple building is a Tainan City monument.

worship:
What to pray for: children's safety and health, protection from evil, and drive in your career. When you need a push to charge ahead, the Third Prince is your god. If the kids at home are a handful, you can ask him to look after them too.

How to worship: bring candy, cookies, cola, and toys (he is a child, after all, and loves sweet and fun things). The three sacrificial meats are fine too, but he prefers snacks. When you offer incense and say your prayer, you can be a little lively; no need to be stiff. Some temples even let you leave a toy car on the altar as an offering. The Third Prince's altar may be the most fun one in Taiwan.

The one taboo: don't disrespect him just because he looks like a child. He is the Marshal of the Central Altar, and his fighting power is first-rate among the gods.
festivals: The 9th day of the 9th lunar month is the Marshal of the Central Altar's birthday. Third Prince temples everywhere hold lively processions, and the energetic Electronic Third Prince performances are the highlight, blending traditional temple troupes with modern electronic music into a temple-festival culture unique to Taiwan.

name: Tiger Lord
domain: Wealth, guarding the home, protecting children (curing mumps)
description: When you enter the temple, don't look up just yet. Bend down and peer beneath the main altar table: crouched there, eyes wide and a coin in its jaws, is a tiger. This is Hu Ye, the Tiger Lord, also called Hu Ye Gong or the General of the Lower Altar. He began as the mount of major gods such as the Earth God, Baosheng Dadi, and the City God, which is why he lives under the altar, yet his incense burns nothing like a mere subordinate's. Taiwanese come to the Tiger Lord for two things above all. The first is wealth: as the saying goes, "the Tiger Lord bites the money home," so worshippers hold coins before his mouth and pass them through the incense smoke to carry fortune home, and the crowds praying for wealth are biggest at Lunar New Year. The second is children: folk belief holds that the Tiger Lord cures "pig-head skin" (mumps) in children and keeps them bright, healthy, and free from harm. The Tiger Lords of Beigang Chaotian Temple, Xingang Fengtian Temple, and Dalongdong Baoan Temple are especially famous. An animal god worshipped in his own right is a sight only Taiwanese folk religion offers.
story:
How did a man-eating tiger become a god? The most popular version involves Baosheng Dadi.

Legend says that Baosheng Dadi (Wu Tao) went into the mountains one day to gather herbs and found a tiger lying by the road, howling in pain. Looking closer, he saw a human bone stuck in its throat. The tiger had hurt a person, and this was karmic retribution. Anyone else would have run, but Baosheng Dadi reached in and pulled the bone from its throat, leaving only a warning: "Never harm a human again."

Once saved, the tiger didn't leave. It chose to stay by Baosheng Dadi's side as his guardian, vowing never to harm people again and instead to protect them with its divine power. It became the Black Tiger General, the Tiger Lord.

Another version stars Celestial Master Zhang, who subdued a fierce tiger terrorizing the mountains, turned it to the right path, and kept it as his attendant; it later became a guardian deity of temples.

A tiger that had hurt people could repent, cultivate itself, and finally become a god. The Tiger Lord's story really carries one of the gentlest beliefs in Taiwanese folk religion: animals have spirit, and even those who went astray can still turn good.

temples.name: Xingang Fengtian Temple
temples.deityStory: Xingang Fengtian Temple's Tiger Lord is one of the best known in Taiwan. Its golden Tiger Lord sits on the altar table, and worshippers mostly come to pray for wealth and for their children's health.

worship:
There's an order to it: offer incense to the main deity first, then worship the Tiger Lord under the altar. The offerings are the most unusual part: raw meat and raw eggs (he is an animal god, and raw food shows respect), candy and cookies (he is also a guardian of children), and some people bring red eggs.

To pray for wealth: hold a coin in front of the Tiger Lord's mouth, pass it over the censer three times while saying "Tiger Lord, bite the money home," then take it home and keep it in your wallet or your home's wealth corner. That is your "mother coin," the seed of your fortune.

To pray for a child's health: write the child's name and birth date and time on red paper, stick it beside the Tiger Lord's altar, then let the child touch his golden statue.

The 6th day of the 6th lunar month is the Tiger Lord's birthday, when many temples hold celebrations. It's the perfect time to bring children for the "passing the Tiger Lord" blessing.
festivals:
**Tiger Lord's Birthday**: the 6th day of the 6th lunar month. Temples that enshrine the Tiger Lord, or whose main deity rides him, hold celebrations with sutra chanting, fire-walking, and banquets. The Tiger Lord birthday rites at Mazu temples such as Beigang Chaotian Temple and Xingang Fengtian Temple are especially grand, and worshippers often bring children for the "passing the Tiger Lord" blessing.

**Praying for wealth at New Year**: Every Lunar New Year, crowds flock to the major temples to ask the Tiger Lord for wealth. Some temples hand out "mother coins" (coins or red envelopes passed over the censer) for worshippers to take home and keep in their wallets or wealth corners for a smooth year.

name: Zhusheng Niangniang
description: You pray to her when you want a child, you pray to her when you're pregnant, and once the baby arrives you pray to her still. Zhusheng Niangniang, the Birth Registrar Goddess, called Zhusheng Ma by Taiwanese, looks after everything from trying to conceive to raising a child. Her domain is wider than you might think: praying for a child, a smooth pregnancy, a safe delivery, and a healthy baby, all under one roof. In temples she is rarely the main deity. She usually sits in a side hall of a Mazu or Guanyin temple, but walk over and you'll see that the incense ash before the side hall is sometimes thicker than in the main hall. Taiwan's birth rate is now the lowest in the world, yet her incense has not dwindled. If anything, because every pregnancy is more precious, every stick of incense is more heartfelt. Many young parents now bring their children too, praying that they'll be easy to raise, rarely sick, and growing strong. The Zhusheng Niangniang halls of Manka Longshan Temple and Lukang Tianhou Temple are always packed with people making wishes around her birthday.
story:
Beside Zhusheng Niangniang's statue usually stand twelve little fairy women, each holding a baby. They are the Twelve Midwives, also called the Twelve Flower Fairies: her delivery team, each with her own role in helping births and child-rearing.

The most intriguing detail is the flowers on her altar. White and red flowers are often placed before her. The traditional explanation is that white flowers stand for praying for a boy and red for a girl (some places say the reverse), so worshippers hoping for a particular sex pay close attention to which flower they touch or take.

The folk stories mostly go like this: someone came to pray to Zhusheng Niangniang for a child, touched a flower almost without thinking, and then really did get pregnant, and the baby turned out to be a boy or girl to match the color of the flower.

Believe it or not as you like. But the steady stream of families coming back each year to give thanks, bringing their children for her to "take a look at," says at least one thing: on the road to having a child, the one Taiwanese trust most is her.
worship:
What to pray for: a child, a stable pregnancy, a smooth delivery, and a child's healthy growth. These days people even come to pray for IVF and fertility treatments to go well.

How to worship: bring fresh flowers, four kinds of fruit, and gold paper. Many people bring sesame-oil chicken with rice wine (the traditional restorative food for new mothers, and the most fitting offering), and some bring tiny clothes and shoes to symbolize welcoming new life. When you offer incense, state your name, age, and situation (trying to conceive, pregnant, or praying for a child's health); the clearer the better. Afterward you can lightly touch the flowers on the altar: white if you hope for a boy, red if you hope for a girl. Customs vary by place, so the temple staff will know best.

The most important rule: if your prayer for a child is answered, you must come back to give thanks, bringing the child to let Zhusheng Niangniang see them and saying thank you. Give back what you asked for, and next time will go just as smoothly.
festivals: The 20th day of the 3rd lunar month is Zhusheng Niangniang's birthday. Temples that enshrine her alongside their main deity hold birthday rites. The Zhusheng Niangniang halls at major temples such as Manka Longshan Temple in Taipei and Lukang Tianhou Temple are especially busy around her birthday, when many worshippers hoping for a child or a safe pregnancy come to make their wishes.

name: Qingshui Zushi (Patriarch of Clear Water)
description: A black-faced statue whose nose "falls off by itself" as a warning: Qingshui Zushi, the Patriarch of Clear Water, popularly called Zushi Gong, the Black-Faced Patriarch, or the Nose-Dropping Patriarch, is one of the most story-filled gods in Taiwan. Born Chen Zhaoying, with the Buddhist name Puzu, he was an eminent Northern Song monk from Anxi in Quanzhou, Fujian, who cultivated, healed the sick, and prayed for rain against drought at Qingshui Cliff, and after his death became the guardian of the Anxi people. In the Ming and Qing dynasties he crossed the strait to Taiwan with migrants from Anxi, Quanzhou. His black face comes from a legend: as he meditated, mountain goblins smoked his face with fire, and though his whole face turned black he did not move. Manka Qingshui Temple, Sanxia Changfu Temple, and Tamsui Qingshui Temple are his three representative temples. The Sanxia temple is famous for its exquisite carving, and its sacred pig ceremony every 6th day of the 1st lunar month is known far and wide.
story:
Almost every legend of Qingshui Zushi comes with a vivid picture.

First, the black face. Legend says that as Chen Zhaoying meditated in the mountains, mountain goblins wanted to drive him away and smoked his face with fire. Deep in meditation, he didn't move at all, letting his whole face be blackened, and in the end he subdued the goblins with compassion. Ever since, every statue of the Patriarch has a black face. That dark face is a badge of being unmoved by anything outside.

Then the rain. One year a great drought struck Anxi; the crops died and the people fell into famine. Chen Zhaoying climbed the mountain himself, set up an altar, and fasted and prayed for rain for seven days and seven nights. On the eighth day, sweet rain fell. From then on the people regarded Qingshui Cliff as holy ground, and the Song court honored him four times, finally with the title "Great Master Zhaoying Guanghui Ciji Shanli."

In Taiwan, Qingshui Zushi gained his most famous marvel: the falling nose. Legend says that whenever plague, earthquake, or war is coming, the nose of the Patriarch's statue drops off by itself as a warning. The Penglai Laozu statue, enshrined in turn by Manka Qingshui Temple and Tamsui Qingshui Temple, is the famous Nose-Dropping Patriarch. A statue that takes off its own nose to wake everyone up: that is how Taiwanese trust in Qingshui Zushi has been passed down, generation after generation.
associatedTemples: Sanxia Changfu Temple (Sanxia District, New Taipei City)
Manka Qingshui Temple (Wanhua District, Taipei City)
Tamsui Qingshui Temple (Tamsui District, New Taipei City)
worship:
Qingshui Zushi was originally an eminent monk, so offerings are mainly vegetarian: fresh flowers, fruit, pastries, and clear tea. It's best to avoid meat (unlike most folk gods, so don't get this wrong).

The busiest season is his birthday on the 6th day of the 1st lunar month, and Tamsui also holds a grand festival on the 6th day of the 5th lunar month, the day he attained the Way. Common rites include passing items over the censer, pilgrimage, and lighting blessing lamps, and the Patriarch temples have a complete set of fortune poems if you want to draw a lot.

The most unusual event is the sacred pig contest held every 6th day of the 1st lunar month at Sanxia Changfu Temple: residents raise sacred pigs for several years, then carry them to the temple on his birthday to compete by weight. In recent years it has sparked debate over animal welfare, but it remains the most important religious event in Sanxia. If you want to see it, get there early on the morning of the 6th.
festivals:
**Qingshui Zushi's Birthday**: the 6th day of the 1st lunar month. This is the most important day in Qingshui Zushi worship, and Patriarch temples all over Taiwan hold celebrations.

**Sanxia Changfu Temple's sacred pig contest, New Taipei**: held every year on the 6th day of the 1st lunar month, a tradition more than a century old. Local residents raise sacred pigs for several years (deliberately fed to push their weight to the limit); on his birthday the pigs are slaughtered, carried before the temple, and ranked by weight. In recent years it has also drawn wide debate over animal welfare.

**Day the Patriarch attained the Way**: the 6th day of the 5th lunar month. Tamsui Qingshui Temple holds its festival on this day, Tamsui's famous "great worship" (Da Bai Bai).

**Lunar New Year**: During the New Year holiday, many families descended from Anxi, Quanzhou migrants come to worship at Patriarch temples. It's an important time to see the social side of Taiwan's migrant faiths.

name: Di Ji Zhu (Foundation Lord)
aliases: Diling Gong (Lord of the Land Spirit)
description: When Taiwanese move into a new home, the first thing they do often isn't cooking a meal. It's setting up a low table by the back door and greeting an unseen "original owner." That owner is Di Ji Zhu, the Foundation Lord, also called Diling Gong or Cuzhai Gong. Traditional belief holds that every piece of land and every house has the spirit of someone who lived there first, and those who come after should worship it regularly, asking permission to live there and for protection of the household. Di Ji Zhu is the most widespread and the most low-key god in Taiwan: there are no great temples, but nearly every household worships him. The rites are distinctly homely too: the offering table faces into the house, it's a low table, and the offerings are home-cooked dishes, made on the 2nd and 16th of each lunar month (zuo ya) and at festivals. City apartment life has worn away many traditions, but most Taiwanese families still insist on worshipping Di Ji Zhu when they move in. It is a new household's most basic greeting to the land's original owner.
story:
Who is Di Ji Zhu? Folk tradition gives three answers.

The most widespread is the "earlier resident" explanation. Every piece of land was once lived on or farmed by someone, and if those earlier residents died with no one to make offerings to them, they stayed attached to the old home and became Di Ji Zhu. If newcomers ignore them, folk belief says the family's luck will go wrong, strange noises will come in the night, and things will move inexplicably. Treat them courteously, though, and Di Ji Zhu rises to become a guardian of the home, driving away evil and misfortune. It all comes down to how you treat him.

The second explanation is tied to Taiwan's ethnic history. During the Ming Zheng period, Han Chinese cleared land on a large scale, and much of it had been villages or burial grounds of the Pingpu (plains indigenous) peoples. To appease the indigenous dead and show respect, the Han developed the ritual of worshipping Di Ji Zhu. This explanation is quite common in Taiwan and carries a cultural meaning of reconciliation between peoples.

The third is more "official": Di Ji Zhu is the household-level counterpart of the Earth God. The Earth God looks after the community, Di Ji Zhu looks after your home, and their roles complement each other.

Whichever version you follow, the heart of it is the same: respect for those who came to the land first. That's why you must worship Di Ji Zhu when you move in. Say hello first, and then you can settle in with peace of mind.
worship:
Worshipping Di Ji Zhu has its own set of rules, quite different from worshipping other gods.

Placement: set the table at the back door or behind the kitchen, facing into the house, so that Di Ji Zhu faces the household. Height: a low stool or low coffee table is enough; you don't use the high table reserved for main deities.

Offerings are home-style: a bowl of white rice, three cups of rice wine, three to five everyday dishes (vegetables or meat), fruit, and three sticks of incense. There's no need for the three sacrificial meats of chicken, duck, and fish. For paper money, burn "four-direction gold" (sifang jin) and silver paper, and not much of it.

When: the 2nd and 16th of each lunar month (zuo ya); festivals such as Lunar New Year, Tomb-Sweeping Day, the Dragon Boat Festival, Ghost Festival, Mid-Autumn, and the Winter Solstice; moving into a new home (the most important, never skipped); and breaking ground, starting work, and finishing work on a house.

After offering incense, remember to say a prayer: introduce your household, explain why you've come, and ask for protection. The whole rite takes about 15 to 30 minutes, the most everyday act of worship in a Taiwanese home.
festivals:
Di Ji Zhu has no particular "birthday," because his worship is household-scale and doesn't call for big festivals. The key times are:

**The 2nd and 16th of each lunar month (zuo ya)**: Traditional businesses and some families worship Di Ji Zhu and the Earth God on the 2nd and 16th of every lunar month. The first of the year, on the 2nd day of the 2nd lunar month, is called "touya" or "kaiya" (the opening ya), and the one on the 16th day of the 12th lunar month is "weiya," the last of the year.

**Lunar New Year (New Year's Eve)**: On New Year's Eve, families worship Di Ji Zhu at the back door, thanking him for a year of protection and asking for a peaceful home in the year ahead.

**The 7th lunar month (Ghost Festival)**: The Ghost Festival is the time for making offerings to wandering spirits with no one to care for them, and many families step up their worship of Di Ji Zhu to keep the home undisturbed.

**Moving in**: New residents must worship Di Ji Zhu on the day they move into a new home, the most widely kept tradition of all in Taiwan. The rite is usually led by an elder of the family or by a hired fortune master.

**Breaking ground, starting and finishing work**: When building a house or doing major renovations, families worship Di Ji Zhu at each key stage and pray for the work to go smoothly.

name: Kaizhang Shengwang (Sacred King of Zhangzhou)
domain: Protector of pioneers, local guardian, warding off evil
description: A Tang dynasty general from 1,300 years ago is still worshipped in Taiwan's temples today. He is Kaizhang Shengwang, the Sacred King Who Opened Zhangzhou, born Chen Yuanguang (657–711) and also called Chen Shengwang or Shengwang Gong. Under Emperor Gaozong of Tang he was sent south to put down unrest, and in Zhangzhou, Fujian, he set up a prefecture and counties, spread farming, and founded schools, so that later generations honored him as the "father of Zhangzhou." When people from Zhangzhou crossed the strait to Taiwan in the Ming and Qing dynasties, they brought their guardian god on board with them. Wherever Zhangzhou settlers cleared land, you often find his temples. Keelung Dianji Temple is the classic example: Keelung's famous Miaokou Night Market grew up right outside the doors of this Kaizhang Shengwang temple. Taoyuan Jingfu Temple also bears witness to Zhangzhou migrants opening up northern Taiwan, and it still holds a grand celebration every year for his birthday on the 15th day of the 2nd lunar month.
story:
In 669, the second year of Emperor Gaozong's Zongzhang era, unrest broke out among the non-Han peoples of southern Fujian, and the court sent Chen Zheng south with his troops to restore order. When Chen Zheng died, command passed to his son Chen Yuanguang, just 21 years old.

What set this young commander apart was that he didn't rely on fighting alone. In Zhangzhou he built beacon towers and garrisoned troops against attack, while at the same time spreading the farming methods of the Central Plains and founding schools, easing the conflict between Han and non-Han peoples through intermarriage, trade, and education. In an age when restoring order meant conquest, he chose a harder and more far-sighted path.

In 711, the second year of the Jingyun era, Chen Yuanguang was killed in battle against Lan Fenggao, at the age of 55. The people of Zhangzhou, grateful for all he had built, raised temples to him of their own accord. Emperor Xuanzong of Tang gave him the posthumous title "Zhongyi Wenhui," Emperor Huizong of Song elevated him to "Kaizhang Zhu Shengwang," and ordinary people honored him as Kaizhang Shengwang.

A thousand years later, when the descendants of Zhangzhou crossed to Taiwan to clear new land, they faced the same unfamiliar ground and the same conflicts, and they brought Kaizhang Shengwang onto the boat with them. The pioneering spirit of a thousand years before took root in Taiwan's soil.

temples.name: Keelung Dianji Temple
temples.deityStory: The birthplace of Keelung's Miaokou Night Market. It enshrines Kaizhang Shengwang as its main deity and is one of Keelung's most important centers of faith.

temples.name: Taoyuan Jingfu Temple
temples.deityStory: The most important temple in central Taoyuan. It enshrines Kaizhang Shengwang as its main deity and bears witness to the history of Zhangzhou migrants opening up Taoyuan.

associatedTemples: Keelung Dianji Temple (Ren'ai District, Keelung City)
Taoyuan Jingfu Temple (Taoyuan District, Taoyuan City)
worship:
The main offerings to Kaizhang Shengwang are fresh flowers, fruit, pastries, and clear tea, and some worshippers prepare the three sacrificial meats. Around his birthday on the 15th day of the 2nd lunar month, temples hold celebrations with sutra chanting, processions, and banquets for the god. It is when his incense burns brightest.

Kaizhang Shengwang is the guardian of the Zhangzhou people, and many communities descended from Zhangzhou keep up the tradition of pilgrimage to the ancestral temple: groups travel to Weihui Temple in Zhangzhou, Fujian, then return to their branch temples in Taiwan. This practice has gradually revived since the lifting of martial law.

At temples in old Zhangzhou migrant settlements, such as Guangji Temple in Zhonghe, New Taipei, you can often see local elders casting moon blocks to consult the god and lighting lamps for blessings on his birthday. If you want to see how the worship organizations of Taiwan's early migrant society actually work, this is the most direct way.
festivals:
**Kaizhang Shengwang's Birthday**: the 15th day of the 2nd lunar month. Temples in communities descended from Zhangzhou hold celebrations including sutra chanting, processions, banquets for the god, and glove puppet performances.

**Pilgrimage to the ancestral temple**: Some temples organize group pilgrimages to Weihui Temple in Zhangzhou, Fujian, around his birthday, one of the important rituals of cultural exchange between Taiwan and Fujian.

**New Year group worship**: During the Lunar New Year, communities descended from Zhangzhou hold group New Year gatherings and worship at Kaizhang Shengwang temples, praying for a peaceful new year and a thriving family. It's an important occasion for seeing the cohesion of Taiwan's early Zhangzhou migrant society.

name: Qi Niang Ma (Seven Mothers)
description: In Tainan, children who have turned 16 crawl under a paper pavilion on Qixi, the seventh night of the seventh month. This is the "Coming of Age at Sixteen" rite, and at its center is Qi Niang Ma, the Seven Mothers, also called the Seven Star Goddess or the Weaving Maiden: seven fairy maidens worshipped together as guardians of children. Taiwanese tradition holds that a child who grows safely to 16 owes it to Qi Niang Ma's protection all along the way. Many families pledge their babies to Qi Niang Ma as godchildren before their first birthday, hanging a charm of coins on red thread around their necks; then on Qixi of the year they turn 16, they return to the temple to remove the charm in thanks, formally marking adulthood. So in Taiwan, Qixi is not just a lovers' day but a day of child protection and coming of age. The custom began on the docks of the Five Canals (Wutiaogang) in old Tainan, where child laborers could only earn full wages once they turned 16. Tainan Kailong Temple is the best-known place for the rite, and every Qixi its ceremonies of crawling under the Qi Niang Ma pavilion and crossing the Qi Niang Ma bridge draw crowds of families.
story:
The main legend of Qi Niang Ma is that of seven fairy maidens who guard the children of the human world.

Legend says the Heavenly Emperor had seven daughters, all compassionate and skilled at weaving. The youngest, the seventh, is the Weaving Maiden everyone knows, famous for coming down to earth and falling in love with the Cowherd, while her six older sisters stayed at work in heaven.

One day the seven maidens learned how many infants in the human world were dying young and how many families were losing their little ones, so together they petitioned the Heavenly Emperor: let us go down and guard the world's children until they grow up safely. Moved by their compassion, he granted their request and allowed them to receive incense under the name Qi Niang Ma. From then on the seven each took on a stage, from birth, first steps, and first lessons to school age and adolescence, guarding the child all the way to adulthood at 16. This is the origin of Taiwan's "Coming of Age at Sixteen" custom.

Another account focuses on the Weaving Maiden herself: she protects not only children but also skill and needlework. Traditionally, women would "beg for skill" on Qixi, setting out offerings and threading needles to ask Qi Niang Ma for nimble hands. This custom has become rare on Taiwan's main island, but it still survives in Kinmen and Penghu.

temples.name: Tainan Kailong Temple
temples.deityStory: Taiwan's most famous Qi Niang Ma temple, and the birthplace and leading temple of the Coming of Age at Sixteen custom.

worship:
Qi Niang Ma is traditionally worshipped mainly by women and children, and the offerings are full of childhood touches: oil rice and sesame-oil chicken (symbols of new life), seven kinds of flowers, seven kinds of fruit, and cotton thread in seven colors (one for each maiden), plus rouge, a mirror, scissors, and needle and thread (carried over from begging for skill on Qixi). The most distinctive is a small paper pavilion, the Qi Niang Ma pavilion.

If you have a child under 16, you can worship for them every Qixi: set out an offering table, burn a Qi Niang Ma pavilion, and hang a protective charm on the child (Qi Niang Ma coins strung on red thread, worn around the neck for safety). On Qixi of the year they turn 16, the charm is removed, announcing the end of childhood.

To see the full rite, go to Tainan Kailong Temple: crawl under the Qi Niang Ma pavilion three times, walk across the Qi Niang Ma bridge, and bow in thanks to Qi Niang Ma. Once it's done, the child has officially come of age.
festivals:
**Qixi (Qi Niang Ma's Birthday)**: the 7th day of the 7th lunar month. In Taiwanese tradition this is an important day for protecting children, and the coming-of-age day for 16-year-olds.

**"Coming of Age at Sixteen" at Tainan Kailong Temple**: held in grand style every year on the 7th day of the 7th lunar month at Kailong Temple in Tainan's West Central District, it is Taiwan's most representative traditional coming-of-age ceremony. The rite includes crawling under the Qi Niang Ma pavilion, crossing the Qi Niang Ma bridge, and parents giving thanks on the child's behalf. It draws large numbers of local families and visitors from elsewhere every year.

**Begging for skill (Qiqiao Festival)**: Traditionally, women asked Qi Niang Ma (the Weaving Maiden) for skillful hands on Qixi. It is rarely seen in Taiwan today.

**Pledging newborns**: Many Taiwanese families take their babies to a Qi Niang Ma temple at one month or one year old for a pledging rite, entrusting the child to Qi Niang Ma's protection until the age of 16.

name: Kuixing Ye (Star Lord of Literature)
description: When exam season comes, one god's altar gets piled high with scallions, garlic, radishes, and zongzi. He is Kuixing Ye, also called Kuidou Xingjun or Dakui Fuzi, the god of scholarly fortune, exam luck, and academic success. "Kui" means "first," and from the imperial exams of old to today's high school entrance exams, college entrance exams, and national civil service exams, students who want to come out on top all pray to him. Kuixing has the strangest look of any god in Taiwan: a ghostly figure with red hair, a blue face, and a golden body, a brush in one hand and a dipper in the other, balanced on one leg. This is the character 魁 taken apart (鬼, "ghost," plus 斗, "dipper"), and it carries the auspicious image of "Kuixing marks the dipper, alone atop the great turtle," meaning first place. In Taiwan, Kuixing is mostly worshipped alongside Wenchang Dijun and Confucius. You can find him in the rear hall of Manka Longshan Temple, in the Wenchang Pavilion of the Tainan Confucius Temple (Kuixing is on the third floor), and in the Wenchang Pavilion at Chihkan Tower (Fort Provintia) in Tainan. The imperial exams were abolished over a century ago, but Kuixing hasn't lost his job: before every exam season, students still line up at his censer, admission tickets in hand.
story:
The legend of Kuixing is a story about judging people by their looks.

It was told in the Song dynasty: there was a scholar of brilliant talent and dazzling writing who failed the exams again and again because he was ugly. He refused to give up, sat the exams again and again, and at last placed first. But when he came before the emperor for the palace examination, the emperor was so shocked by his face that he wanted to strip him of his title.

The scholar defended himself before the throne, neither humble nor arrogant: "Your servant's face may be ugly, but his learning shines like the sun and moon. If you choose men by their looks, how will you win over the scholars of the realm?" Then, on the spot, he wrote a rhapsody and set out his views on governing the nation. The emperor was won over completely. Here was a man whose talent could "take first place among all the scholars of the realm," and he named him top scholar.

This scholar was later honored as Kuixing, the symbol of choosing scholars for talent, not for looks. One explanation says his ghostly appearance comes from exactly that unremarkable face. Being ugly doesn't matter; with real learning, even an emperor has to bow.

Another explanation comes from the character itself: 魁 is made of 鬼 ("ghost") and 斗 ("dipper"), and the first four stars of the Northern Dipper are together called "Kui," so Kuixing is the leading star of the Dipper and governs the scholarly fortunes of the world. Both explanations survive today, one about a person's determination, the other about a star in the sky.
worship:
Offerings to Kuixing are full of puns: scallions (cong, for clever), garlic (suan, for good at calculating), radish (caitou, for good luck), zongzi (for passing), cake (gao, for high scores), and apples (ping, for taking the exam in peace). A whole table of offerings adds up to one blessing.

Students can also bring their admission tickets and stationery to pass over the censer, circling them three times above it to borrow a little of Kuixing's spiritual power. Some temples offer a "Kuixing brush" you can take home, symbolizing flowering writing and flowing ideas.

When you pray, spell out the subjects you're taking and the scores you're aiming for, and say how you plan to work for them. Kuixing worship is about "people and god working together": he gives you a boost, but you still have to do the studying. When the results come out and you've made it, remember to bring offerings back to the temple to give thanks.
festivals:
**Kuixing's Birthday**: the 7th day of the 7th lunar month. Chihkan Tower in Tainan holds a Kuixing ceremony every year around Qixi.

**Before major exam seasons**: Before each January (college entrance exam), May (junior high comprehensive assessment), July (advanced subjects test), and year-end (civil service and national exams), Kuixing and Wenchang temples everywhere fill with students and parents. Students are advised to go about a week before the exam to avoid the busiest times.

**Giving thanks after success**: After results are announced, many students who got into the school or job they wanted bring offerings back to the temple to fulfill their vows, and families coming just to give thanks are a common sight around Kuixing temples.

name: Tudipo (Earth God's Wife)
domain: Family harmony, marital love, urging people to keep their feet on the ground
description: Many people worshipping the Earth God deliberately skip the old woman beside him. She is Tudipo, the Earth Grandmother, also called Tudi Gongpo, the Earth God's consort. Folk opinion holds that she "won't hand out favors": legend says she is shrewd and practical and often advises the Earth God not to scatter wealth carelessly among people. But that bad reputation is unfair. Tudipo guards something else: family harmony, love between husband and wife, and the least popular but most solid lesson of all, keeping your feet on the ground. Some see her as the embodiment of a homemaker's wisdom. You can find Tudipo at Sijie Fude Temple in Wujie, Yilan, and at Hongludi Nanshan Fude Temple in Zhonghe, where the Earth God and Tudipo were carved together from a single stone. Her statues usually show a kindly old woman, hair in a bun, holding a staff or a gold ingot, sitting quietly beside the Earth God. Next time you worship the Earth God, don't forget to greet her too.
story:
Why does Tudipo carry the blame for "refusing to make people rich"? A classic folk story explains it.

Legend says that when the Jade Emperor sent the Earth God down to look after a stretch of land, he asked him what he wished for. The kind-hearted Earth God answered, "May everyone in the world be rich and at peace."

Tudipo, standing beside him, quickly shook her head. "That won't do! If everyone were rich, who would carry the sedan chairs, who would till the fields, who would sweep the floors? If everyone lived in comfort, how would the world keep running?"

The Jade Emperor found this very sensible. So the world came to have rich and poor, high and low, each person meeting a different lot according to karma and effort. And Tudipo has carried the blame ever since; many people simply pass her by when they worship the Earth God.

But look at it another way: was she wrong? What Tudipo stands for isn't stinginess but the wisdom of social order and the division of labor. Without the cold water she poured, the world would lose its reason to work hard.

Another version says Tudipo was a virtuous mortal woman who ran her household well and raised her children wisely, and after death was made the Earth God's consort. In either version, she is the practical one who keeps the household going.

temples.name: Hongludi Nanshan Fude Temple
temples.deityStory: The Earth God and Tudipo here were carved together from a single stone.

worship:
Tudipo is usually worshipped together with the Earth God: offer incense to the Earth God and tell him your concerns, then say it all again to Tudipo. Offerings are mainly fresh flowers, fruit, pastries, and clear tea, and people who want to do it properly prepare two sets, one for each.

What should you ask her for? Family harmony, a good marriage, dutiful children. These "family matters" are her specialty. It's also common to come when moving into a new home or newly married and ask the two of them together to protect the household.

One small reminder: when telling Tudipo about family matters, be respectful, and don't complain about or criticize your family. Tradition says she will remember what you say and use it as the basis for judgment later. Some temples have a separate censer in front of her statue, so you can worship her on her own as well.
festivals:
**Tudipo's Birthday**: the 17th day of the 3rd lunar month (some say the 16th day of the 4th lunar month). The date varies by temple tradition, so check the local temple's announcements in advance.

**Earth God's Birthday**: the 2nd day of the 2nd lunar month (touya) and the 15th day of the 8th lunar month (Mid-Autumn); weiya falls on the 16th day of the 12th lunar month. On these days Earth God temples hold celebrations, and Tudipo is usually worshipped alongside him. Many families also bring offerings to the Earth God temple on these days.

**Lunar New Year**: Many worshippers make a special trip to the Earth God temple over the Lunar New Year to worship the Earth God and Tudipo together, praying for a peaceful home and good fortune in the new year.

name: Wen Wu Dazhong Ye
domain: Finding lost things, settling lawsuits, warding off evil, upholding justice
description: In the seventh lunar month, offering tables across Taiwan stretch from front doors all the way to temple squares, and the guests of honor aren't gods but the "good brothers," the wandering spirits. Presiding over this pact between the living and the dead is Wen Wu Dazhong Ye, the Civil and Martial Lords of the Multitude, also called Dazhong Ye or Lao Da Gong. "Dazhong" means "the many, without distinction": the spirits of those who died far from home in war, plague, or disaster, with no descendants to make offerings, are gathered and enshrined together, given a resting place and a share of incense, turning from homeless ghosts into the recognized Dazhong Ye. It is one of the gentlest inventions of Taiwanese folk religion: even the forsaken dead deserve dignity. Dazhong Ye temples are found mostly on old battlefields, in places once hit hard by plague, and in remote frontier settlements, and Xinzhuang Dizang An is one of the representative temples. Every year at the Ghost Festival's Pudu, from a single table at a family's front door to grand rites at the temples, all of Taiwan practices this same compassion, feeling others' hunger and suffering as its own.
story:
The story of Dazhong Ye is the story of the disasters of Taiwan's early migrants.

In the Ming and Qing dynasties, Han Chinese crossed the strait to Taiwan, only to lose their lives again and again to miasma, plague, armed clan feuds, pirates, and natural disasters. Many died far from home with no one to bury them. Partly out of humanity and partly out of awe (fearing the restless dead), local residents began to gather and bury the remains together and build temples to make offerings. This was the origin of Dazhong Ye temples.

Manka has a representative story. During the Xianfeng reign of the Qing (1854–1855), plague swept through Manka with terrible loss of life, and migrants from Hui'an in Quanzhou brought Lingan Zunwang, the Qingshan King, from their hometown to suppress it. Legend says that on the night the Qingshan King was carried in procession, the plague really did recede, and in 1856 the residents built a temple to him.

Dazhong Ye is not the legend of any one god, but the embodied collective memory of a whole migrant society: of death, of disaster, and of reconciliation.
associatedTemples: Xinzhuang Dizang An (Xinzhuang District, New Taipei City)
worship:
Offerings to Dazhong Ye differ a little from those for other gods. The three sacrificial meats, rice cakes, fruit, and wine are all fine (meat is no problem), and many families prepare a whole chicken or pig's trotters. But one offering belongs to him alone: "water rice," white rice with water, meant to feed the good brothers. Some people also light Pudu lamps to light the way for wandering souls.

On ordinary days you can visit a Dazhong Ye temple on your own to pray for safety, release from trouble, and wealth. The seventh lunar month is the main event, the Ghost Festival's Pudu, held jointly by households and temples, the largest act of worship in Taiwan. Toucheng in Yilan also holds "Grappling with the Ghosts" (qianggu), where competitors climb tall greased towers to seize the offerings. It's a spectacular sight.

Remember the taboos: no frivolous talk or laughing during worship; during Pudu, don't step on offerings and don't say the word "ghost." Call them "good brothers." If you want to photograph the rites, ask the temple's permission first.
festivals:
**Ghost Festival (Dazhong Ye's Pudu)**: the 15th day of the 7th lunar month. This is the most important day in Dazhong Ye worship. Dazhong Ye temples and households all over Taiwan hold the "**Ghost Festival Pudu**," inviting the "good brothers" to enjoy the offerings. Pudu ranges in scale from individual families (an offering table at the front door) to township-level grand rites at the temples.

**Manka Qingshan Temple's night patrol**: Every year on the nights of the 20th and 21st of the 10th lunar month, the "**Qingshan King's Night Patrol**" is held; the formal daytime procession follows on the 22nd, and the 23rd is the Qingshan King's birthday. The procession winds through Manka at night, with firecrackers and drums and gongs going all night long. In 2010 it was registered as a folk cultural asset of Taipei City.

**Grappling with the Ghosts in Toucheng, Yilan**: Held every year at the end of the 7th lunar month (as the Ghost Festival Pudu draws to a close) in Toucheng, Yilan, it is Taiwan's most representative qianggu ritual. Competitors climb greased towers to seize the offerings at the top. Liu Mingchuan banned it in the Qing dynasty, and after the war it was interrupted again under martial law; only after martial law was lifted did it return as a regular event, and today it is an internationally known folk event.

The whole seventh lunar month is known in Taiwan as "**Ghost Month**," when Dazhong Ye worship is at its most active. The Pudu rites of temples and households everywhere form a complete folk system, an important field for studying how traditional Taiwanese society viewed life and death.

name: Door Gods
domain: Guarding doorways, warding off evil spirits and ghosts
description: Walk into any temple in Taiwan, and the first gods you "meet" aren't inside the hall at all. They're painted on the doors: the Door Gods. Taiwan's most common pair are the Tang dynasty generals Qin Shubao (white-faced, with phoenix eyes, holding a mace) and Yuchi Gong (black-faced and glaring, holding a steel whip). Legend says they once guarded Emperor Taizong of Tang's palace gate through the night to drive off ghosts, and they have been painted on countless front doors ever since. Besides this pair of "martial door gods," there are civil-official door gods holding court tablets; Shentu and Yulei, found in the Lunheng's quotation of the Classic of Mountains and Seas; the "promotion and rank" door gods symbolizing rising office and wealth; and eunuch, palace-maid, and child door gods guarding the rear halls. In Taiwan, temple door gods are a hand-painted traditional craft, and works by master painters such as Pan Li-shui and Chen Yu-feng are seen as a measure of a temple's artistic worth. Door gods for homes are mostly printed and replaced before Lunar New Year, part of clearing out the old and bringing in the new. To judge a temple, look at its doors first: the quality of the door gods is often the temple's calling card.
story:
The story of the door gods begins with an emperor who couldn't sleep.

Legend says Emperor Taizong of Tang, Li Shimin, after years of war and much killing, was haunted after taking the throne by nightly dreams of vengeful ghosts coming for his life. Terrified and sleepless, he let the affairs of state all but grind to a halt, and none of the imperial physicians' remedies worked.

The great generals Qin Shubao and Yuchi Gong volunteered. In full armor, one on the left and one on the right, they stood guard outside his bedchamber all night. Strangely enough, from that night on the ghosts dared not come near, and Taizong finally slept soundly.

But there was a problem: after many nights on guard, even men of iron couldn't keep it up. Unwilling to see his beloved generals wear themselves out, Taizong came up with a solution. He had the court painters make full-length portraits of the two in their imposing battle dress and pasted them on the doors of his bedchamber. The ghosts saw the portraits from afar and still dared not approach.

As word spread, ordinary people rushed to copy him, pasting portraits of the two generals on their own doors. And once pasted, they stayed for more than a thousand years, right down to today's Lunar New Year.

Earlier door gods appear in the Classic of Mountains and Seas as quoted in the Lunheng by Wang Chong of the Eastern Han: beneath a great peach tree on Mount Dushuo in the Eastern Sea, two gods, Shentu and Yulei, caught ghosts and fed them to tigers. But for sheer drama, the pair of real men replaced by their portraits, Qin and Yuchi, won people's hearts, and they became the most popular door gods in Taiwan.
worship:
Home door gods are changed on a fixed schedule: after the gods are sent off on the 24th day of the 12th lunar month and before New Year's Eve, the old door gods are taken down and burned and new ones are pasted up, marking out with the old and in with the new. There's one key taboo when hanging them: the two door gods must face each other (faces turned inward toward one another), never back to back, or folk belief says they lose their protective power.

Hand-painted temple door gods don't need special offerings day to day, but every few years painters are called in to restore them; when a major temple is renovated, a traditional "door god consecration" is held, dotting the eyes with a vermilion brush to give the door gods their spirit. Folk belief also holds that if a home has been troubled for a long time, you can have a Taoist priest perform a rite and then hang new door gods to drive out the bad energy and settle the home.

When you visit a temple, remember not to step on the threshold or linger on it as you pass through the gate. At some temples the custom is for men to enter and leave on the left and women on the right, matching the positions of the two door gods. That's the most basic courtesy you can show them.
festivals:
**Lunar New Year (time to hang the door gods)**: Traditionally, door god pictures are changed after the "sending off the gods" day on the 24th of the 12th lunar month and before New Year's Eve. It is one of the key steps in a Taiwanese family's year-end cleaning and New Year decorating, and together with spring couplets, red envelopes, and the New Year's Eve dinner it forms the core of Lunar New Year customs.

**A note**: Door gods have no single shared birthday. As gods with a "job," their worship belongs to that of the main deity or the household, so there are few festivals held specifically for door gods.
